newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Latam expected U.S. arms after praise and pressure.
newsitem.headline: Latam expected U.S. arms after praise and pressure.

text.p: Latin America had expected a change in Washington's ban on advanced arms sales ahead of President Bill Clinton's visit in October, after praise for the region's stability and pressure from U.S. arms makers.

Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. John Shalikashvili called Latin America a "dream come true" for its resolution of regional conflicts during his tour of Mexico, Brazil, Argentina and Chile last week.

But defence experts said lobbying from U.S. manufacturers helped make the decision inevitable after Peru bought Russian MiG-29 fighter jets last year -- which President Alberto Fujimori showed off for the first time this week.

While Shalikashvili said in public a review of the 20-year-old ban -- imposed by the Carter regime when most of the region was under military rule -- was not yet complete, in private he told his hosts he was "optimistic," said one Argentine military man who spoke to the top U.S. officer.

"Thanks for the good news," said another Argentine senior officer on hearing that Clinton was ready to lift the "presumption of denial" that has been imposed on all Latin American requests for U.S. arms sales for two decades.

"It means we can enter the circuit once again," said the officer, after Washington officials said the region "has become like the rest of the world" with armed forces mostly under civilian control and border disputes under control.
Argentina's immediate aim would be to get spare parts for military hardware rendered immobile by the ban, such as M113 transports "missing spark plugs to, well, everything."
"Most of all this is tacit recognition to the stability of the region, to our democratic regimes, and of the fact that there is no arms race in the region," he said.
The policy change throws open to U.S. arms manufacturers a region eager to modernise its out-of-date military hardware.
"It was absolutely foreseeable that this would happen especially after Peru's purchase of the MiGs," said Chilean defence expert Eduardo Santos.

Chile, the region's big military spender, has had to replenish stocks with European suppliers and, while showing interest in U.S. F-16 fighter planes, was looking elsewhere at French Mirage-2000s and Swiss Grippens.

In a strong hint of change to come, in April Clinton authorised U.S. firms to submit bids to Chile for the purchase of fighters. The timing of the ban being lifted was crucial for U.S. manufacturer McDonnell Douglas which had a mid-August deadline for making an offer to the Chilean air force.

"For Chile it's positive as when there are more suppliers competing, prices will be better," said Santos. "The decision returns military relations between Chile and the United States to normal, which is a positive advance."

At a meeting of Western Hemisphere defence ministers in Argentine last October, some countries including Argentina told then U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry they feared a a change in U.S. policy could unleash a regional arms race.
Perry promised any sales would be carefully monitored on a "case-by-case basis" with "restraint" as the catchword.
